one_sentence_story: By recording directly across the giant 1-millimetre neurons of the sea snail Aplysia starting in 1970, Eric Kandel proved that short-term memory chemically tunes existing synapses while spaced long-term learning activates CREB genes to physically double synaptic connections — winning the 2000 Nobel Prize.
so_what_for_you: Give your brain spaced practice sessions plus protein-consolidating sleep: short cramming sessions only turn up temporary chemical volume, whereas spaced sessions give CREB time to build real new synaptic hardware.

jargon_map.plain: minutes-long chemical boost at existing terminals (cAMP/PKA) versus days-to-lifetime structural growth of brand-new synaptic terminals (CREB + protein synthesis)
jargon_map.analogy: turning up a speaker's volume knob temporarily vs wiring in twice as many speakers

jargon_map.plain: marine sea snail possessing only ~20,000 giant, color-identifiable neurons up to 1 mm across
jargon_map.analogy: nature's magnifying glass for memory neurobiology

jargon_map.plain: dialing down a reflex to harmless repeated taps (1,300 to 850 terminals) vs amplifying defense after an alerting stimulus (1,300 to 2,600 terminals)
jargon_map.analogy: tuning out ticking radiator noise vs snapping alert after a near-miss

jargon_map.plain: nuclear gene-transcription accelerator (CREB-1) and brake (CREB-2) deciding whether an experience gets built into permanent synaptic structure
jargon_map.analogy: the master architect signing off on permanent remodeling

jargon_map.plain: Craig Bailey & Eric Kandel's electron-microscope proof that long-term memory physically doubles terminal count on the sensory neuron
jargon_map.analogy: when 'rewiring your brain' stopped being a figure of speech
